claim: AWS strongly recommends IKEv2 for a Site-to-Site VPN connection and says to use IKEv1 only if the customer gateway device does not support IKEv2.
q: Which IKE version does AWS recommend for Site-to-Site VPN?
v: only use IKEv1 if your customer gateway device does not support IKEv2
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/cgw-best-practice

We strongly recommend using IKEv2 for your Site-to-Site VPN connection. IKEv2 is a simpler, more robust, and more secure protocol than IKEv1. You should only use IKEv1 if your customer gateway device does not support IKEv2.

claim: If you place the customer gateway behind a router or firewall that does NAT, you give AWS the public IP address of the NAT device.
q: What IP address do you use for a customer gateway device that sits behind a NAT device?
v: You will use the public IP address of your NAT device
you use the public IP address of the NAT device
scope: customer gateway behind a router or firewall
ev: www/vpn/faqs
You will use the public IP address of your NAT device.

claim: If you do not plan to use NAT-T, you must disable it on your device. Otherwise AWS tries to establish the tunnel over UDP port 4500, and the tunnel does not establish if that port is not open.
q: What happens if NAT-T is enabled on the device but UDP port 4500 is not open?
v: we will attempt to establish a tunnel over UDP port 4500
If that port is not open the tunnel will not establish
scope: NAT traversal on the customer gateway device
ev: www/vpn/faqs

You will need to disable NAT-T on your device. If you don’t plan on using NAT-T and it is not disabled on your device, we will attempt to establish a tunnel over UDP port 4500. If that port is not open the tunnel will not establish.

claim: If the customer gateway device is behind a firewall or other device that uses NAT, it must have an identity (IDr) configured.
q: What must a customer gateway device behind a NAT device have configured when AWS initiates IKE?
v: it must have an identity (IDr) configured
behind a firewall or other device using Network Address Translation (NAT)
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/initiate-vpn-tunnels
If your customer gateway device is behind a firewall or other device using Network Address Translation (NAT), it must have an identity (IDr) configured.

claim: The AWS VPN service is route-based. If a device uses a policy-based solution, you need to limit it to a single security association.
q: Does Site-to-Site VPN support policy-based VPN devices?
v: the service is a route-based solution
you will need to limit to a single SA
ev: www/vpn/faqs

The AWS VPN service is a route-based solution, so when using a route-based configuration you will not run into SA limitations. If, however, you are using a policy-based solution you will need to limit to a single SA, as the service is a route-based solution.

claim: A device that supports dynamically routed Site-to-Site VPN connections must be able to establish BGP peering, bind tunnels to logical interfaces (route-based VPN), and use IPsec Dead Peer Detection.
q: What must a customer gateway device support for a dynamically routed VPN connection?
scope: customer gateway devices for dynamically routed connections
ev: www/vpn/faqs

In addition to the above capabilities, devices supporting dynamically-routed Site-to-Site VPN connections must be able to:
Establish Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) peering
Bind tunnels to logical interfaces (route-based VPN)
Utilize IPsec Dead Peer Detection

claim: If the customer gateway device supports BGP, specify dynamic routing. If the device does not support BGP, specify static routing.
q: When do you choose dynamic routing and when static routing for a Site-to-Site VPN connection?
v: If your customer gateway device supports Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), specify dynamic routing
If your customer gateway device does not support BGP, specify static routing
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/vpn-static-dynamic

If your customer gateway device supports Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), specify dynamic routing when you configure your Site-to-Site VPN connection. If your customer gateway device does not support BGP, specify static routing.

claim: AWS recommends BGP-capable devices when available, because BGP offers robust liveness detection checks that can help failover to the second VPN tunnel when the first goes down.
q: Why does AWS recommend BGP-capable customer gateway devices for Site-to-Site VPN?
v: We recommend that you use BGP-capable devices, when available
robust liveness detection checks that can assist failover to the second VPN tunnel
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/vpn-static-dynamic

We recommend that you use BGP-capable devices, when available, because the BGP protocol offers robust liveness detection checks that can assist failover to the second VPN tunnel if the first tunnel goes down.

claim: With a device that does not support BGP advertising, you select static routing and enter the IP prefixes of your network. With a BGP device you do not specify static routes, because the device advertises its routes itself.
q: What do you enter for a Site-to-Site VPN connection with static routing, and what with BGP?
v: you must select static routing and enter the routes (IP prefixes) for your network
you don't specify static routes to the Site-to-Site VPN connection
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/vpn-static-dynamic

If you use a device that supports BGP advertising, you don't specify static routes to the Site-to-Site VPN connection because the device uses BGP to advertise its routes to the virtual private gateway. If you use a device that doesn't support BGP advertising, you must select static routing and enter the routes (IP prefixes) for your network that should be communicated to the virtual private gateway.

claim: The VPC route table uses the most specific route that matches the traffic (longest prefix match). A local route is preferred over overlapping propagated routes from a VPN or Direct Connect connection, even if the propagated routes are more specific.
q: Which route wins in a VPC route table when routes overlap, and how do propagated VPN routes compare with the local route?
v: the most specific route in your route table that matches the traffic
the local route is most preferred even if the propagated routes are more specific
scope: VPC route table with propagated routes
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/vpn-route-priority

We use the most specific route in your route table that matches the traffic to determine how to route the traffic (longest prefix match). If your route table has overlapping or matching routes, the following rules apply:
If propagated routes from a Site-to-Site VPN connection or Direct Connect connection overlap with the local route for your VPC, the local route is most preferred even if the propagated routes are more specific.

claim: When the prefixes are the same, a virtual private gateway prefers BGP routes from a Direct Connect connection first, then manually added static routes of a Site-to-Site VPN connection, then BGP routes from a Site-to-Site VPN connection.
q: For the same prefix, which path does a virtual private gateway prefer: Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN?
v: BGP propagated routes from an Direct Connect connection
Direct Connect BGP routes come first
from most preferred to least preferred
scope: virtual private gateway route selection for identical prefixes
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/vpn-route-priority

If the prefixes are the same, then the virtual private gateway prioritizes routes as follows, from most preferred to least preferred:
BGP propagated routes from an Direct Connect connection
Blackhole routes are not propagated to a Site-to-Site VPN customer gateway via BGP.
Manually added static routes for a Site-to-Site VPN connection
BGP propagated routes from a Site-to-Site VPN connection

claim: For matching prefixes where each Site-to-Site VPN connection uses BGP, the prefix with the shortest AS PATH is preferred.
q: How are BGP routes compared when several Site-to-Site VPN connections advertise the same prefix?
v: the prefix with the shortest AS PATH is preferred
scope: Site-to-Site VPN connections that use BGP
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/vpn-route-priority
For matching prefixes where each Site-to-Site VPN connection uses BGP, the AS PATH is compared and the prefix with the shortest AS PATH is preferred.

claim: The health of a tunnel endpoint takes precedence over other routing attributes, for VPNs on virtual private gateways and on transit gateways.
q: What takes precedence over other routing attributes when a VPN tunnel is selected?
v: The health of a tunnel endpoint takes precedence over other routing attributes
VPNs on virtual private gateways and Transit Gateways
scope: VPNs on virtual private gateways and transit gateways
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/vpn-route-priority
The health of a tunnel endpoint takes precedence over other routing attributes. This precedence applies to VPNs on virtual private gateways and Transit Gateways.

claim: When a propagated VPN or Direct Connect route has the same destination CIDR block as an existing static route, the static route is preferred (for example a route whose target is an internet gateway or virtual private gateway).
q: Which route is used when a propagated route and a static route have the same destination CIDR block?
v: have the same destination CIDR block as other existing static routes
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/vpn-route-priority

If propagated routes from a Site-to-Site VPN connection or Direct Connect connection have the same destination CIDR block as other existing static routes (longest prefix match cannot be applied), we prioritize the static routes whose targets are an internet gateway, a virtual private gateway, a network interface, an instance ID, a VPC peering connection, a NAT gateway, a transit gateway, or a gateway VPC endpoint.

claim: On a virtual private gateway, one tunnel across all VPN connections on the gateway is selected, and ECMP is not supported. ECMP is supported for Site-to-Site VPN connections on a transit gateway.
q: Can a virtual private gateway use several VPN tunnels at once with ECMP?
v: ECMP is not supported for Site-to-Site VPN connections on a virtual private gateway
ECMP, which is supported for Site-to-Site VPN connections on a transit gateway
scope: virtual private gateway versus transit gateway
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/vpn-route-priority

For a virtual private gateway, one tunnel across all Site-to-Site VPN connections on the gateway will be selected. To use more than one tunnel, we recommend exploring Equal Cost Multipath (ECMP), which is supported for Site-to-Site VPN connections on a transit gateway. For more information, see Transit gateways in Amazon VPC Transit Gateways. ECMP is not supported for Site-to-Site VPN connections on a virtual private gateway.

claim: On a transit gateway you can use ECMP to get higher VPN bandwidth by aggregating several VPN tunnels. The VPN connection must use dynamic routing; ECMP is not supported with static routing.
q: What routing type does ECMP across VPN tunnels require?
v: the VPN connection must be configured for dynamic routing
ECMP is not supported on VPN connections that use static routing
scope: Site-to-Site VPN connections on a transit gateway
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/vpn-limits

For Site-to-Site VPN connections on a transit gateway, you can use ECMP to get higher VPN bandwidth by aggregating multiple VPN tunnels. To use ECMP, the VPN connection must be configured for dynamic routing. ECMP is not supported on VPN connections that use static routing.

claim: In the VPC route table you add a route for the remote network with the virtual private gateway as target. You can also enable route propagation so that network routes are added to the table automatically.
q: How do VPN routes get into the VPC route table when you use a virtual private gateway?
v: you must add a route for your remote network and specify the virtual private gateway as the target
enable route propagation for your route table
scope: VPC route table of a VPC with a virtual private gateway
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/vpn-route-priority

In your VPC route table, you must add a route for your remote network and specify the virtual private gateway as the target. This enables traffic from your VPC that's destined for your remote network to route via the virtual private gateway and over one of the VPN tunnels. You can enable route propagation for your route table to automatically propagate your network routes to the table for you.

claim: An accelerated Site-to-Site VPN connection uses AWS Global Accelerator to route traffic from your on-premises network to the AWS edge location closest to your customer gateway device.
q: What does an accelerated Site-to-Site VPN connection do?
v: uses AWS Global Accelerator to route traffic
an AWS edge location that is closest to your customer gateway device
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/accelerated-vpn

An accelerated Site-to-Site VPN connection (accelerated VPN connection) uses AWS Global Accelerator to route traffic from your on-premises network to an AWS edge location that is closest to your customer gateway device.

claim: Acceleration is supported only for Site-to-Site VPN connections attached to a transit gateway. Virtual private gateways do not support accelerated VPN connections.
q: Which target gateway supports an accelerated Site-to-Site VPN connection?
v: Acceleration is only supported for Site-to-Site VPN connections that are attached to a transit gateway
Virtual private gateways do not support accelerated VPN connections
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/accelerated-vpn
Acceleration is only supported for Site-to-Site VPN connections that are attached to a transit gateway. Virtual private gateways do not support accelerated VPN connections.

claim: An accelerated Site-to-Site VPN connection cannot be used with an AWS Direct Connect public virtual interface.
q: Can an accelerated Site-to-Site VPN be used over a Direct Connect public virtual interface?
v: cannot be used with an AWS Direct Connect public virtual interface
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/accelerated-vpn
An Accelerated Site-to-Site VPN connection cannot be used with an AWS Direct Connect public virtual interface.

claim: You cannot turn acceleration on or off for an existing Site-to-Site VPN connection. You create a new connection with acceleration on or off, point the device to it, and delete the old connection.
q: Can you convert an existing Site-to-Site VPN connection to an accelerated one?
v: You cannot turn on or turn off acceleration for an existing Site-to-Site VPN connection
create a new Site-to-Site VPN connection with acceleration on or off as needed
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/accelerated-vpn

You cannot turn on or turn off acceleration for an existing Site-to-Site VPN connection. Instead, you can create a new Site-to-Site VPN connection with acceleration on or off as needed. Then, configure your customer gateway device to use the new Site-to-Site VPN connection and delete the old Site-to-Site VPN connection.

claim: By default, acceleration is disabled when you create a Site-to-Site VPN connection; you can enable it when you create a new VPN attachment on a transit gateway.
q: Is acceleration on or off by default for a new Site-to-Site VPN connection?
v: You can optionally enable acceleration when you create a new Site-to-Site VPN attachment on a transit gateway
cond: enable at creation on a transit gateway attachment
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/accelerated-vpn
By default, when you create a Site-to-Site VPN connection, acceleration is disabled. You can optionally enable acceleration when you create a new Site-to-Site VPN attachment on a transit gateway.

claim: NAT traversal is required for an accelerated VPN connection and is enabled by default. IKE negotiation for accelerated tunnels must be initiated from the customer gateway device.
q: Which side must start IKE on an accelerated VPN tunnel, and is NAT-T required?
v: NAT-traversal (NAT-T) is required for an accelerated VPN connection and is enabled by default
IKE negotiation for accelerated VPN tunnels must be initiated from the customer gateway device
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/accelerated-vpn
NAT-traversal (NAT-T) is required for an accelerated VPN connection and is enabled by default.
docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/accelerated-vpn
IKE negotiation for accelerated VPN tunnels must be initiated from the customer gateway device.

claim: AWS creates and manages two accelerators for an accelerated VPN connection, one for each tunnel. You cannot view or manage them in the AWS Global Accelerator console or APIs.
q: Who manages the accelerators of an accelerated Site-to-Site VPN connection?
v: we create and manage two accelerators on your behalf, one for each VPN tunnel
AWS manages two accelerators, one per tunnel
You cannot view or manage these accelerators yourself
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/accelerated-vpn

When you create an accelerated VPN connection, we create and manage two accelerators on your behalf, one for each VPN tunnel. You cannot view or manage these accelerators yourself by using the AWS Global Accelerator console or APIs.

claim: Accelerated Site-to-Site VPN makes the user experience more consistent by using the highly available and congestion-free AWS global network instead of multiple public internet networks.
q: Why use an accelerated Site-to-Site VPN?
v: the highly available and congestion-free AWS global network
ev: www/vpn/faqs

VPN connections face inconsistent availability and performance as traffic traverses through multiple public networks on the internet before reaching the VPN endpoint in AWS. These public networks can be congested. Each hop can introduce availability and performance risks. Accelerated Site-to-Site VPN makes user experience more consistent by using the highly available and congestion-free AWS global network.

claim: AWS VPN CloudHub lets several Site-to-Site VPN connections give your sites secure communication with each other, not only with the VPC. It uses a hub-and-spoke model that works with or without a VPC and is suited to branch offices that already have internet connections.
q: What is AWS VPN CloudHub?
v: operates on a simple hub-and-spoke model that you can use with or without a VPC
This enables your sites to communicate with each other, and not just with the resources in your VPC
scope: multiple Site-to-Site VPN connections to one virtual private gateway
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/VPN_CloudHub

If you have multiple AWS Site-to-Site VPN connections, you can provide secure communication between sites using the AWS VPN CloudHub. This enables your sites to communicate with each other, and not just with the resources in your VPC. The VPN CloudHub operates on a simple hub-and-spoke model that you can use with or without a VPC.

claim: For VPN CloudHub you create one virtual private gateway and a dynamically routed VPN connection from each customer gateway. You must use a unique BGP ASN for each customer gateway, and the sites must not have overlapping IP ranges.
q: What does VPN CloudHub require for the customer gateways and the site address ranges?
v: You must use a unique Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) Autonomous System Number (ASN) for each customer gateway
The sites must not have overlapping IP ranges
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/VPN_CloudHub
Create multiple customer gateways, each with the public IP address of the gateway. You must use a unique Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) Autonomous System Number (ASN) for each customer gateway.
docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/VPN_CloudHub
The sites must not have overlapping IP ranges.

claim: VPN CloudHub is suitable if you have multiple branch offices with existing internet connections and want a convenient, potentially low-cost hub-and-spoke model for primary or backup connectivity between the sites.
q: When is AWS VPN CloudHub a suitable design?
v: suitable if you have multiple branch offices and existing internet connections
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/VPN_CloudHub

This design is suitable if you have multiple branch offices and existing internet connections and would like to implement a convenient, potentially low-cost hub-and-spoke model for primary or backup connectivity between these sites.

claim: To protect against the loss of the customer gateway device, set up a second Site-to-Site VPN connection to the same virtual private gateway by adding a second customer gateway device. If one device fails, the virtual private gateway sends all traffic to the working device.
q: How do you protect a Site-to-Site VPN against a failed customer gateway device?
v: set up a second Site-to-Site VPN connection to your VPC and virtual private gateway by adding a second customer gateway device
the virtual private gateway directs all traffic to the working customer gateway device
scope: Site-to-Site VPN on a virtual private gateway
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/vpn-redundant-connection

To protect against a loss of connectivity in case your customer gateway device becomes unavailable, you can set up a second Site-to-Site VPN connection to your VPC and virtual private gateway by adding a second customer gateway device.
docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/vpn-redundant-connection

Both devices should advertise the same IP ranges to the virtual private gateway. We use BGP routing to determine the path for traffic. If one customer gateway device fails, the virtual private gateway directs all traffic to the working customer gateway device.

claim: Private IP VPN lets you deploy IPsec VPN over Direct Connect, which encrypts traffic between your on-premises network and AWS without public IP addresses or additional third-party VPN equipment.
q: What is a private IP Site-to-Site VPN over Direct Connect?
v: deploy IPsec VPN over Direct Connect, encrypting traffic between your on-premises network and AWS
without the use of public IP addresses or additional third-party VPN equipment
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/private-ip-dx

With private IP VPN, you can deploy IPsec VPN over Direct Connect, encrypting traffic between your on-premises network and AWS, without the use of public IP addresses or additional third-party VPN equipment.

claim: Private IP Site-to-Site VPN works over a Direct Connect transit virtual interface and uses a Direct Connect gateway and a transit gateway.
q: Which Direct Connect virtual interface and gateways does a private IP VPN need?
v: works over an Direct Connect transit virtual interface (VIF)
It uses an Direct Connect gateway and a transit gateway
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/private-ip-dx

Private IP Site-to-Site VPN works over an Direct Connect transit virtual interface (VIF). It uses an Direct Connect gateway and a transit gateway to interconnect your on-premises networks with AWS VPCs.

claim: Before private IP VPN, encrypting traffic over Direct Connect meant using a public virtual interface, which needs public IP addresses for VPN endpoints. Private IP VPN allows the encryption over a transit virtual interface with private IPs instead.
q: Why use private IP VPN instead of a VPN over a Direct Connect public virtual interface?
v: had to use a public Direct Connect virtual interface (VIF) for encrypting traffic over Direct Connect
encryption over Direct Connect transit VIFs (instead of public VIFs)
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/private-ip-dx
Previously, customers had to use a public Direct Connect virtual interface (VIF) for encrypting traffic over Direct Connect, which requires public IP addresses for VPN endpoints.
docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/private-ip-dx
The private IP VPN feature allows encryption over Direct Connect transit VIFs (instead of public VIFs), coupled with the ability to configure private IPs.

claim: You need a transit gateway to deploy private IP VPN connections, and a private IP VPN attachment on the transit gateway requires a Direct Connect attachment for transport.
q: Do you need a transit gateway for a private IP VPN?
v: you need a Transit gateway to deploy private IP VPN connections
requires a Direct Connect attachment for transport
ev: www/vpn/faqs
Yes, you need a Transit gateway to deploy private IP VPN connections. Also, a private IP VPN attachment on Transit Gateway requires a Direct Connect attachment for transport.

claim: Site-to-Site VPN Concentrator is suited to customers who need to connect 25+ remote sites to AWS with low bandwidth per site, under 100 Mbps. Concentrators are supported only with Transit Gateway, not with Cloud WAN or a virtual private gateway.
q: What is a Site-to-Site VPN Concentrator and which target gateway does it support?
v: connect 25+ remote sites to AWS, with each site needing low bandwidth (under 100 Mbps)
25+ remote sites with low bandwidth each
VPN Concentrators are only supported with Transit Gateway
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/vpn-concentrator
VPN Concentrator is suitable for customers who need to connect 25+ remote sites to AWS, with each site needing low bandwidth (under 100 Mbps).
docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/vpn-concentrator
VPN Concentrators are only supported with Transit Gateway. This feature is not supported with Cloud WAN or Virtual Private Gateway.

claim: Site-to-Site VPN Concentrators support BGP routing only. Static routing is not supported.
q: Which routing type does a Site-to-Site VPN Concentrator support?
v: support BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) routing only
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/vpn-concentrator
Site-to-Site VPN Concentrators support BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) routing only. Static routing is not supported.

claim: IPv6 traffic is not supported for VPN connections on a virtual private gateway. IPv6 for outer tunnel IPs is supported only on Transit Gateway and Cloud WAN.
q: Which target gateways support IPv6 for Site-to-Site VPN?
v: IPv6 traffic is not supported for VPN connections on a virtual private gateway
IPv6 for outer tunnel IPs is only supported on Transit Gateway and Cloud WAN
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/VPC_VPN
IPv6 traffic is not supported for VPN connections on a virtual private gateway. IPv6 for outer tunnel IPs is only supported on Transit Gateway and Cloud WAN.

claim: A single VPN connection cannot carry both IPv4 and IPv6 traffic; you need separate connections. You also cannot enable IPv6 on an existing connection; you must delete it and create a new one.
q: Can one Site-to-Site VPN connection carry IPv4 and IPv6 traffic, and can an existing one be converted to IPv6?
v: A single Site-to-Site VPN connection cannot support both IPv4 and IPv6 traffic simultaneously
You cannot modify an existing IPv4 VPN connection to use IPv6
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/VPC_VPN
A single Site-to-Site VPN connection cannot support both IPv4 and IPv6 traffic simultaneously. You need separate VPN connections to transport IPv4 and IPv6 packets.
docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/VPC_VPN
You cannot modify an existing IPv4 VPN connection to use IPv6. You must delete the existing connection and create a new one.

claim: By default, a Site-to-Site VPN connection supports IPv4 traffic inside the VPN tunnels. You can configure a new connection on a transit gateway to support IPv6 traffic inside the tunnels instead.
q: What IP version does a Site-to-Site VPN connection carry inside the tunnels by default?
v: By default, a Site-to-Site VPN connection supports IPv4 traffic inside the VPN tunnels
You can configure a new Site-to-Site VPN connection to support IPv6 traffic inside the VPN tunnels
scope: Site-to-Site VPN connection on a transit gateway
cond: IPv6 inside the tunnels needs a new connection
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/ipv4-ipv6
By default, a Site-to-Site VPN connection supports IPv4 traffic inside the VPN tunnels. You can configure a new Site-to-Site VPN connection to support IPv6 traffic inside the VPN tunnels.

claim: CloudWatch collects raw VPN data into near real-time metrics for VPN tunnels, and the statistics are recorded for a period of 15 months.
q: How long are Site-to-Site VPN CloudWatch statistics kept?
v: recorded for a period of 15 months
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/monitoring-cloudwatch-vpn

You can monitor VPN tunnels using CloudWatch, which collects and processes raw data from the VPN service into readable, near real-time metrics. These statistics are recorded for a period of 15 months, so that you can access historical information and gain a better perspective on how your web application or service is performing.

claim: Site-to-Site VPN logs give details on IPsec tunnel establishment, IKE negotiations, DPD messages, and BGP status and routing updates, and they can be published to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
q: Which logs does Site-to-Site VPN provide and where can they be published?
v: details on IP Security (IPsec) tunnel establishment, Internet Key Exchange (IKE) negotiations, dead peer detection (DPD) protocol messages
Site-to-Site VPN logs can be published to Amazon CloudWatch Logs
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/monitoring-logs

AWS Site-to-Site VPN logs provide you with deeper visibility into your Site-to-Site VPN deployments. With this feature, you have access to Site-to-Site VPN connection logs that provide details on IP Security (IPsec) tunnel establishment, Internet Key Exchange (IKE) negotiations, dead peer detection (DPD) protocol messages, Border Gateway protocol (BGP) status and routing updates. Site-to-Site VPN logs can be published to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.

claim: Tunnel endpoint lifecycle control gives you control over when AWS managed tunnel endpoint replacements happen. Use it if you have short-term business needs or can only support a single tunnel per VPN connection.
q: What does tunnel endpoint lifecycle control let you do?
v: control over the schedule of endpoint replacements
accept AWS managed updates to tunnel endpoints at a time that works best for your business
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/tunnel-endpoint-lifecycle

Tunnel endpoint lifecycle control provides control over the schedule of endpoint replacements, and can help minimize connectivity disruptions during AWS managed tunnel endpoint replacements. With this feature, you can choose to accept AWS managed updates to tunnel endpoints at a time that works best for your business. Use this feature if you have short-term business needs or can only support a single tunnel per VPN connection.

claim: With tunnel endpoint lifecycle control enabled, you receive AWS Health notifications for upcoming tunnel endpoint replacements. If you do not apply the update before the Maintenance auto applied after time, AWS replaces the endpoint soon after.
q: How are you notified of upcoming Site-to-Site VPN tunnel endpoint replacements?
v: You will receive AWS Health notifications for upcoming tunnel endpoint replacements
AWS will automatically perform the tunnel endpoint replacement
ev: docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/tunnel-endpoint-lifecycle
You will receive AWS Health notifications for upcoming tunnel endpoint replacements.
docs/vpn/latest/s2svpn/tunnel-endpoint-lifecycle
If you do not apply updates before the Maintenance auto applied after date, AWS will automatically perform the tunnel endpoint replacement soon after, as part of the regular maintenance update cycle.
